claims.text: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 exhibits excellent or large caloric performance.
The untreated alloy has poor mechanical integrity and is prone to cracking.
Post-solidification liquid-metal infiltration can introduce a ductile Cu binder into the alloy.
The proposed Cu content is approximately 5–10 vol%.
A temperature around 1100°C is just above the melting point of Cu.
Processing near 1100°C can remain well below temperatures that destabilize the MM′X phase.
An inert Ar atmosphere will avoid or limit oxidation during infiltration.
Controlled Cu infiltration will form an interconnected Cu phase along grain boundaries and discrete binder regions.
The Cu phase will bridge microcracks and mitigate stress concentrations in the MM′X matrix.
The Cu binder network will arrest crack propagation and redistribute applied stress.
Cu's high thermal conductivity will help maintain efficient heat transport relevant to caloric operation.
Adding only a minor Cu volume fraction will leave the intrinsic caloric phase largely unaltered.
Cu infiltration will significantly improve the alloy's mechanical integrity.
The Cu-infiltrated alloy will achieve a compressive strength greater than 218 MPa.
The highest previously reported compressive strength for an epoxy-containing comparison sample was 218 MPa.
The Cu-infiltrated alloy will retain adiabatic temperature and entropy changes similar to those of the pristine alloy.
Limiting Cu to 5–10 vol% will avoid excessive dilution of the caloric phase.
Excessive processing temperature, time, or interdiffusion could harm the alloy's performance.
The modified alloy is intended to sustain caloric performance during cyclic applied-field and pressure-field operation from room temperature to moderate elevations.
Optimizing Cu fraction and heat-treatment parameters may be required to balance mechanical integrity against caloric-response retention.
